title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The core failure here is one of training data provenance. Suno admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified YouTube, Deezer, and Genius as specific scraping sources. When the resulting system is prompted with details specific enough to evoke a known song, it can reproduce that song's melody, lyrics, and arrangement closely enough that record labels were able to demonstrate the reproduction repeatedly in court filings. That is a model memorizing and regurgitating copyrighted material, not a system that learned abstract musical structure free of the source content.

The failure sits at the data-collection and training stage, before any user ever touched the product. A rights-clearance review of training data, or filtering to detect and exclude copyrighted recordings, could have been points of intervention. Neither appears to have been in place. A German court has ruled against Suno in the GEMA case, Warner Music settled its lawsuit and formed a joint venture with Suno, and Universal Music settled its Udio lawsuit, but the US class actions from independent artists and the Round Hill suits against Suno remain active proceedings.

What is not established is that any finding in one jurisdiction resolves the legal questions in another, that settlements constitute admissions of wrongdoing, or that allegations of deliberate concealment of training data have been proven as fact in a court verdict.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and others have filed separate lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno. The companies are accused of copying thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models. The record labels claim both companies have been deliberately secretive about their training data and that their business model relies on exploiting copyrighted material on a massive scale. The lawsuits name specific artists whose work was allegedly used, including The Beatles, Michael Jackson, and many others.

To support their claims, the record labels demonstrated they could repeatedly recreate versions of famous copyrighted songs by using specific prompts in both AI generators. For example, prompting Suno with details about Mariah Carey and holiday music produced a near-identical copy of "All I Want for Christmas Is You," while an Udio prompt about 2004 alternative rock generated a song that replicated Green Day's "American Idiot" lyrics and melody. The lawsuits were filed in New York and Massachusetts and include a thumb drive of AI-generated music examples as evidence.
